summary: Presents NERD, an experimental database for LISP and a discussion of how to deliver endpoint-identifier to routing-locator mappings to routers in a reliable, scalable and secure way. It takes a push approach, with the whole database distributed rather than looked up on demand.

eli5.summary: Instead of phoning for every address you need, you get a copy of the whole phone book delivered and kept up to date.

questions: how can lisp mappings be distributed to routers
how does nerd scale to millions of addresses
subtitle: A database that delivers LISP mappings from endpoint addresses to network locations.

tldr.problem: LISP needs to map endpoint addresses (EIDs) to routing locations (RLOCs) at scale, and doing it on-demand is slow and increases packet loss. A system that reliably distributes these mappings to routers is needed.
tldr.mechanism: NERD is an experimental database that takes a push approach: the entire mapping database is distributed to routers via HTTP, with periodic updates delivered as diffs, and all data is signed for integrity.
tldr.outcome: This approach scales to at least 100 million mappings and reduces the number of packets dropped waiting for mapping lookups, though no operational deployments were known at publication.

today: RFC 6837 is Experimental and has not been superseded. The RFC is based on experiments from 2007–2009, and the author was not aware of operational NERD deployments at publication. The specification remains available for implementation and evaluation but has not become widely adopted in LISP deployments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6837 presents NERD (Not-so-novel EID-to-RLOC Database), an experimental system for delivering LISP mapping data to routers. LISP, defined in RFC 6830, separates the addresses that hosts use (Endpoint IDs or EIDs) from the network addresses routers advertise (Routing Locators or RLOCs). This separation reduces the state that must change in the core Internet when a site moves, but routers need to know the mapping between EIDs and RLOCs to forward packets.

Rather than having routers look up mappings on demand (the pull model), NERD pushes the entire database to routers and then distributes updates as changes occur. This approach aims to reduce dropped packets that would result from waiting for mapping lookups to complete. The RFC is based on experiments performed between 2007 and 2009, and the author notes that no operational NERD deployments were known at the time of publication.
sections.eli5: Imagine your router needs to send a letter to an address it has never seen before. Instead of stopping to ask the post office every time (slow!), NERD gives your router a giant directory of all addresses it might ever need, updated regularly.

sections.title: How NERD Works
sections.content:
NERD operates in two parts: initial database distribution and ongoing updates. When a router first comes online, it retrieves the entire database via HTTP from a known server. The router is preconfigured with trusted certificates and verifies both the database's signature and the authority's public key before installing it. If verification fails, the router tries other sources.

Periodically, routers poll for new versions by requesting a version number file. If the local version is out of date, the router requests a change file that lists new, modified, or deleted mappings since the router's current version. Change files use the same record format as the full database, making them easy to parse and integrate. The system supports multiple databases managed by different authorities, allowing databases to be merged as long as no EID appears in more than one database.
sections.eli5: First you get the whole phone book. Every so often you call to see if there's a new version. If there is, you get a list of only the changes since you last checked, rather than a whole new book.

sections.title: Database Format and Records
sections.content:
The NERD database consists of a header and signed records. The header contains a schema version, a database version number, the database name (as a DNS identifier), and a PKCS#7 authentication block holding the signature and the database authority's certificate. Records are sorted by address family and EID, with prefix length as a secondary key.

Each mapping record contains the number of routing locators, the EID and its prefix length, and one or more RLOC entries, each with priority, weight, and an address family identifier. The minimum record size is 16 bytes for IPv4 and 30 bytes for IPv6, with each additional routing locator adding 8 or 20 bytes respectively. The database supports multiple databases with different authorities, each identified by a DNS name in the header.
sections.eli5: A record in the database says: 'This address block belongs to this network location, and here are backup locations if the first one fails, in order of preference.'

sections.title: Scalability and Performance
sections.content:
NERD is designed to scale to 100 million mappings. At that scale with four routing locators per mapping and IPv6 addresses, the database would be approximately 9 GB. A router downloading this at 100 MB/s would take 80 seconds; slower links would require proportionally longer. The RFC includes detailed analysis of server requirements: with 10 million routers and 10% daily change, approximately 10,000 servers with 1 GB/s links each would be needed to complete hourly updates in about 300 seconds.

The key assumption underlying NERD's design is that mapping data changes infrequently—only when provisioning or configuration changes occur, not on link failures. This static nature of the data is crucial to the approach's viability. The RFC explicitly states that NERD alone cannot handle host mobility and must be paired with other mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The math checks out: even with billions of addresses, modern networks can push the database to all routers in reasonable time, as long as the mappings don't change constantly.

sections.title: Security and Integrity
sections.content:
The integrity and authenticity of NERD mappings are critical: if an attacker can forge or tamper with the database, traffic can be redirected to any destination. NERD addresses this through object-level signing using X.509 certificates and PKCS#7. Routers are preconfigured with trusted certificate authority certificates and verify both the database authority's certificate and the signature on every database and update file.

The RFC proposes a trust model where a small number of database authorities (perhaps IANA or regional registries) manage EID-to-RLOC mappings, reducing the number of entities each router must trust from O(N²) to O(number of authorities). The RFC discusses risks including private key compromise, for which the mitigation is revocation via a certificate revocation list distributed alongside databases. The system uses SHA1 and RSA signatures; the RFC notes that cryptographic message syntax (CMS) was recommended for future work but was not widely deployed at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: Every database is signed by an authority you trust, so you can verify no one tampered with the mappings in transit.
